overview: Andwa, also written Andoa, communities live in the Amazonian borderlands of Ecuador and Peru. Many speak Kichwa while maintaining a distinct Andwa identity. Their history includes mission pressures, rubber exploitation, divided families and collective efforts to recover Katsakati, their ancestral language.

periods.title: War divides families
periods.summary: The Ecuador-Peru war fragmented Andwa territory and separated relatives across the border. This rupture restricted community connections for decades; it did not erase Andwa identity.

periods.title: Recognition and organization
periods.summary: Andwa organizing gained official recognition in Ecuador in 2003. Language, territory and political representation became closely connected in the nationality’s public work.

periods.title: A binational reunion
periods.summary: NAPE’s life plan records a 2008 gathering in Puka Yaku that reunited Andwa communities from Ecuador and Peru. Participants developed a shared agenda for territorial, cultural and organizational work.

periods.title: Recording remembered speech
periods.summary: Visits to Peruvian communities located people who remembered Katsakati. Researchers recorded Hipólito Arahuanaza in Kapawari in 2010, producing material for linguistic analysis and teaching.

periods.title: From documentation to teaching
periods.summary: After Arahuanaza’s death, language work continued through workshops. Participants used existing records to develop vocabulary, stories and classroom activities, although important gaps in documentation remained.

periods.title: Potters teach across communities
periods.summary: Andwa women from the Dagua family in Canelos taught university participants about ceramic work. Their collaboration brought pottery, oral expression and public workshops into a shared educational project.

periods.title: A dictionary presented publicly
periods.summary: The Andwa nationality and Nature and Culture International presented Kupukwano at Amazon State University in February 2023. Leaders and young people attended the dictionary launch.

items.text: NAPE’s life plan describes household livelihoods that combine cultivated gardens, fishing, hunting, gathered fruit and small livestock. Gardens include cassava, plantains, maize, peanuts and peppers. These activities connect family provisioning to different parts of the forest and river landscape.

The plan records pottery-making alongside the weaving of bags, baskets, hammocks and fishing nets. Such objects served practical domestic and river tasks as well as exchange. Its account also recognizes migration for wage work, rather than portraying community life as isolated from wider economies.

Community authorities described in the plan organize collective work, maintain shared property and address internal disputes. They coordinate with NAPE’s governing council. This arrangement brings local responsibilities together with representation to provincial and national institutions; the plan distinguishes these connected levels of government.

sections.title: Finding and teaching an ancestral language

items.text: During 2009 fieldwork, María Santi, Dionisia Arahuanaza and Lidia Arahuanaza helped researchers check remembered vocabulary. In Kapawari, Hipólito Arahuanaza contributed recorded narratives in 2010, with Kichwa mediation. Documentation depended on Indigenous memories and multilingual collaboration, not simply on an outsider locating an unknown language.

Funding difficulties interrupted further recording, and researchers learned of Arahuanaza’s death in 2012. The surviving material included narratives with sometimes incomplete Kichwa translations. These limitations matter: a recording collection preserves valuable speech without providing a complete account of every word, grammatical pattern or social use.

In the December 2013 Quito workshop, participants wrote stories and dramatized selected examples for video recording. Teaching resources included vocabulary cards, dice, interactive posters and a teacher’s guide. The activities connected language learning with meaningful situations and creative work.

The Dagua family women who hosted a 2016 university project identified as Andwa and spoke Kichwa. They made mukawas, tinajas, callanas and human-shaped ceramic figures. Calling themselves weavers, they shaped vessels with lengths of clay, demonstrating a skilled process that students learned through participation.

The collaboration linked pottery with spoken stories, music, bodily expression and visual design. At Interactos in Guayaquil in November 2016, students presented a short documentary, information booklets and edited oral texts. Five women from Canelos and a Kichwa translator participated in a workshop and conversation.

Kupukwano, the Andwa language dictionary, was publicly introduced on February 16, 2023 by Daniel Dagua, then president of the nationality. The project partner describes a gathering of leaders, representatives and young people at Amazon State University. The publication is a concrete resource for language work, not evidence that everyone has regained fluency.

Erika Rosado’s 2022 to 2023 interviews examine how leaders use Katsakati in public life, including greetings before continuing in Kichwa or Spanish. The research links these practices with claims to recognition and territory. It treats language recovery as political and cultural work, not a simple test of authentic identity.

ending.text: Andwa communities continue through political organization, skilled work and language recovery. The loss of an elder speaker did not mean the disappearance of the people. The imported map’s endpoint in 1500 is a coverage limit, not an extinction date or an end to this history.
